Like the rest of our core preparations, Resonance has a “Use Global Soundset” button in the top left, a “Reset Mods” button in the top right, Mute (M) and Solo (S) buttons in the bottom right, and level meters and sliders for Send and Main along the righthand side of the pop-up window.

***“Fundamental” and “Keys for Closest Partials”***  
The “fundamental” is the key we use to set the fundamental for the partial/overtone structure we want. In the default setup, it is set to C0 (imagine we are holding down the key for  a low low C, below the bottom of the familiar 88-key keyboard). The “keys for closest partials” are the ones that, when struck, will be closest to the overtones of the “fundamental,” causing it to ring. In the default setup, these are set to the first 8 partials of C0. Of course, that overtone structure is not limited to C; all “fundamentals” will have a similar, transposed set of closest partials.”

This arrangement allows for the creation of all sorts of “overtone” structures, including “undertones” and totally unnatural “inharmonic” structures. Try, for instance, setting the fundamental to anything other C0 and leaving everything else the same, and then try playing various combinations of held and struck keys and listen to the resonances. 

***Offsets***  
These values (in cents) set how far the tuning of the “resonant key” string is from the tuning of the actual overtone of the “held key” string. As in the example above, striking the equal tempered Bb4 while holding down C2 will result in two quite different Bb’s; the 7th partial of the “held key” C2 is 31 cents flat to the equal tempered Bb4 “resonant key.” Mousing over that Bb (Bb2 in the Offsets keyboard) will reveal the \-31c offset; the “keys” on this graphical keyboard are sliders that you can drag on to change the offset, and you can also “edit all” to change by typing. 

***Gains***  
The various partials of a vibrating string have varying strengths, some naturally louder or softer than others. The Gains keyboard enables building that into the resonant structure of Resonance

***Overlap Sensitivity***  
sets how sensitive the system is to overlapping of partials. With high sensitivity, partials will respond to other partials that are quite far away, whereas with low sensitivity, the partials have to line up more precisely to create resonance

***Stretch***  
Stretches the overtone structure, akin to the octave stretching that happens in real piano strings (Railsback stretching). This sort of inharmonicity can be subtle, as the effect becomes more pronounced the further you go from the fundamental.

***Presence***  
Adjusts the relative intensity and attack of the sympathetic resonance; lower presence will be more gentle and subtle, higher presence will have a stronger attack.

***Sustain***  
Adjusts the sustain time of the sympathetic resonance. Note that longer sustain times will impact the CPU load of Resonance, resulting in more overlapping sustained notes. 

***Envelope***  
Controls the ADSR envelope of the sympathetic resonance.

***Presets Menu***  
Set to “PianoLow” by default, this offers a range of presets for overtone structures. Some of these are based on measurements drawn from William Sethares’ book [*Tuning, Timbre, Spectrum, Scale*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b138848)*.*

***Attached Tuning***  
If a Tuning preparation is attached to Resonance, that will set how the fundamentals (held keys) are tuned. So, for instance, in the example above considering C2 and Bb2:

![][image59]

Both the C2 and Bb2 are equal tempered, so the 7th partial of C2 is noticeably lower than the 4th partial of Bb2. If, however, the Tuning preparation is set to “C partial,” then the Bb2 will be tuned like the 7th partial of C:

![][image60]

and now the 7th partial of C2 will line up precisely with the 4th partial of Bb2. This can get pretty complex quickly, especially if, say, the Direct and Resonance preparations are using different Tunings. 

As should be clear, the aim here is to allow for a range of explorations of sympathetic resonance; it should be possible to make something that sounds quite “natural,” which could be of use when making a recording of bitKlavier, or just to give the instrument a kind of warm glow; but it is also possible to create a range of other kinds of sympathetic structures, perhaps modeled after the spectral qualities of different kinds of instruments (gamelan, for instance), undertones, or…. who knows. Overall, this is a keyboard-centric approach to thinking about sympathetic resonance, where depressed keys allow for a range of resonant pitches that can be excited by other keys.

| Tuning |
| :---- |

### What is it?

The Tuning preparation is another of the control features which sets bitKlavier apart from both the acoustic piano and the more conventional sampler. Tuning provides a hugely flexible array of musical and compositional opportunities, from creating and manipulating a custom temperament to manually editing the precise pitch of every key on the keyboard. 

### How to make a Tuning Preparation

To add a Tuning preparation to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Tuning.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut ‘,’ and the Tuning will appear in the Construction site. Double-click on the Tuning preparation, and you’ll see the pop-up window displayed below. By default, it is in “Static” Tuning mode, but selecting different modes will display different parameters.

### Navigating the Tuning Preparation

#### Temperament

A temperament is essentially a one-octave tuning scheme that adjusts certain intervals in order to prioritize consonance between them. A temperament is repeated *every* octave of the keyboard. The root of the temperament can be determined by the user — more on that soon. 

![][image61]

The drop-down menu in the middle contains presets for different tunings. Full charts for these tunings are located in the [Appendix at the end of the manual](#appendix). The default temperament is Equal Temperament: Click the drop-down menu and select “Just” temperament. Note how the temperament keyboard will visually change to reflect how each interval has been tuned from Equal Temperament. **Blue** means flat, **Red** means sharp, and the intensity of the color reflects the degree to which a pitch has been raised or lowered from ET.  
![][image62]

Each key can be manually adjusted: Go back to Equal Temperament, click D, and begin to drag *up* while holding the mouse down. Notice that several things change: As the D becomes more red to indicate a rise in pitch, the temperament changes from Equal Temperament to Custom. The pitch of each key can also be changed by clicking at various locations on the surface of each key. 

The “cents from ET” window at the upper end of the temperament keyboard, which shows the specific amount the pitch has been altered, changes in real time as well. Play along the keyboard, and notice that every D is now pitched quite a bit higher. 

Let’s say we want to create a temperament where every G is lowered by 8 cents. Simply select G on the temperament keyboard and type \-8.0 into the “scale” window. Now play C5 and G5 on your MIDI keyboard, and note that 5th doesn’t sound quite as “perfect” as it does in ET. Go along the keyboard and you will find that every G is now slightly lower. 

You’ll notice an asterisk on C. This indicates that C is the root, meaning that the temperament is generated using a fixed scheme of offsets beginning on C. Try selecting Duodene from the drop-down menu. Notice that the first few notes of the temperament are slightly raised, while the last few notes of the temperament are slightly lowered. Now, change the root of the temperament to E, and notice how this pattern is translated 4 semitones higher.

For greater depth and control, all 12 notes in a temperament can be quickly edited via a text field. With Equal Temperament selected, click “Edit all” to reveal a field of 0s. Each of these corresponds to the current pitch value of each ascending note in the temperament. 

Change the first few numbers and click “Edit all” again (or press the return key) to view the temperament keyboard; note the visual changes based on the values you typed. 

A slider below the temperament keyboard moves the entire pitch of the keyboard up or down. To quickly raise the pitch of the keyboard, move the slider to the right, or change the “offset” pitch to a higher number (the unit is cents). Type 100 or \-100 into the “offset” box to immediately raise or lower the temperament keyboard a semitone. 

#### Semitone Width

Changing the semitone width in bitKlavier can lead to some wild results. Semitone width simply translates to “number of cents in every semitone,” or half step. By default, this value is 100\. Changing this value to 200 means that every semitone on the keyboard is now a whole step. By extreme contrast, changing this value to \-100 inverts the keyboard. As you ascend the physical keyboard, the pitch becomes lower. 

Of course, the “semitone width” feature can be used in more subtle ways as well. Change the value to 102, which adds 2 cents to every semitone. Over two octaves, the notes are spaced \+48 cents apart, nearly a quarter-tone. This could be a subtle effect or a powerful compositional device depending on your application and intention. Note that the semitone width applies to the entire range of the keys selected in the Keymap preparation. To have a segment of the keyboard with a different semitone width, you will need to create two Keymaps with different ranges or pitches selected, and route them to different Tuning preparations.

Adjusting the semitone width while *also* using a non-Equal Temperament system has some wild results. For example, if you create a quarter-tone Piano using a semitone value of 50c, try setting the tuning to Just intonation. When you play C4 to Ab4, ordinarily a minor sixth, you’ll end up with a Just-tuned major third. Check out the [Tuning and Temperament](https://www.kadenze.com/courses/reinventing-the-piano-i/sessions/tuning-and-temperament#) session from “Reinventing the Piano” for more information. 

#### Semitone Root

Under “semitone width” there is also a drop-down menu for “semitone root.” This sets a specific note to Equal Temperament as a starting point for a non-100-cent semitone scheme. By default, C4 will sound at ET as expected, with subsequent half-steps generated from there. But any pitch can serve as that initial reference, and can actually change the range of available notes on the keyboard. 

For example, Set the semitone width to 50, creating a quarter-tone keyboard, and play some notes around middle C. Then change the root to D4. In the first case, C will actually sound a C, and in the second D will actually sound a D. 

Another example: Let’s say you want to perform with a violinist who tunes to A440, but you want to use a quarter-tone Piano. If you set the semitone width to 50, simply set the root to A4, so that A4 can be used to “tune” bitKlavier. Starting on A4, the violin and bitKlavier will both be at 440hz, then the bK keyboard will be in quarter-tones above and below the new root of A4.

Note that the root is only relevant if the semitone width is significantly larger or smaller than 100\. At 101 or 99, you won’t hear much of a change within the few surrounding octaves.

#### Full Keyboard Tuning 

Along the bottom of the Tuning preparation there is a full 88-key keyboard. As in the Keymap preparation, each key corresponds to exactly one pitch, so unlike editing on the Temperament keyboard, any edits made on the lower keyboard will apply to a single pitch. Think of this as absolute tuning versus circular tuning: Tuning by temperament is circular (repeated every octave), while tuning individual notes is absolute tuning and is not translated or repeated anywhere else on the keyboard. 

Any key along the bottom keyboard can be individually tuned by click-dragging, by clicking at a certain location on the surface of the key, or by adjusting the pitch in the “Individual Key Offsets” keyboard. Here’s the result of some random clicking:

![][image63]

Note that when you mouse over the lower keyboard, the note’s relative offset will appear in the text box to the right. 

IMPORTANT: any changes made to the absolute tuning of the keyboard happen *in addition* to the existing temperament\! Example: If every E is raised 14 cents in the temperament, and E4 is lowered by 8 cents on the absolute keyboard, then E4 will still be 6 cents sharp, while every other E will still be 14 cents sharp. 

For more control, each key can be individually edited in a text field. Open the “Edit All” field and type **60:-13.7** in the empty space. Press return or hit “Edit All” again to return to the keyboard view; you will see that middle C (MIDI value 60\) has been lowered \-13.7 cents *relative to the temperament tuning.* This makes it easy to edit note values. These values can be copied into bitKlavier from other programs.

### The Spiral

The spiral provides a way to visualize the tuning relationships of currently active notes. For this to work, in your Piano, Keymap must be connected to Tuning *as well as* Direct, so that Tuning knows what notes to display in real time. 

![][image64]

The spiral begins inside with the lowest note on the piano and gradually circles outwards to the highest note. Active notes appear as circles near the equal-tempered references, with numbers indicating how far they diverge from ET, and lines between notes show the interval between them, in cents.

![][image65]

Loosely inspired by [Erv Wilson’s logarithmic spiral](http://www.anaphoria.com/harm&Subharm.pdf), the motivations for having the spiral will become evident later when we look at *spring tuning*, but even just as a way to quickly see how notes are tuned it is quite useful.

### Adaptive Tuning

Temperaments are fixed systems. We can pre-plan changes on the fly using Piano maps and Modifications, but conceptually, temperaments are inherently static. By contrast, *adaptive tunings* change in direct response to what you play. The tuning and temperament continuously regenerate based on your playing via a limited set of constraints. While these processes can be used to create “optimal” tunings–systems that minimize idiosyncratic intervals–based on your playing, they are also intended for exploration and play, and as such can yield unexpected results. bitKlavier currently has three basic flavors of adaptive tuning. 

With both **Adaptive Tuning 1** and **Adaptive Anchored Tuning 1**, the fundamental (root) of the established adaptive scale (set with the menu to the left of the Tuning window) will shift automatically, either after a certain number of notes have been played (the Maximum slider parameter) or after a certain amount of time has passed (the Threshold slider parameter). Each note is immediately re-tuned based on a moving fundamental, and various parameters determine *when* the fundamental should move and *where* it should move. In your Piano, Keymap must be connected to Tuning *as well as* Direct, so that Tuning knows what notes to adjust in real time.

#### Adaptive Anchored Tuning

In the Adaptive Anchored system, when either of the adaptive parameters are exceeded (History or Threshold), the fundamental will change to the tuning determined by the “Anchor” scale. To begin, set History to 1, meaning that the fundamental will reset with every note played. Set “Threshold” to 1000 (for reasons to be clear shortly), “Adaptive scale” to Just, and “Anchor scale” to Equal Tempered. Now, play an *ascending* scale. You should hear an Equal Tempered scale where the “current fundamental” changes to a new integer value with each note you play. You should also see that the “note” (to the bottom left about the big keyboard) is always an integer (Equal Tempered) value.

Now set History to 2 and try playing a scale again. As long as each note is within 1000ms of the previous note, you should see the “current fundamental” change with every *other* note played, and that the “note” values of the in-between notes will have some fractional value; this is where the system starts to kick in. With these same settings, try this:

1. Play C4 then Bb5 (an ascending minor-7th) and listen to the tuning of the Bb  
2. Play D4 then Bb5 (an ascending minor-6th); hear how the Bb is tuned differently\!

In (1) C4 is the fundamental, so the Bb is tuned as a 7/4 minor-7th above C, which is about 31 cents flatter than an Equal Tempered minor-7th.   
In (2) D4 is the fundamental, so the Bb is tuned as a 8/5 minor-6th above D, which is about 14 cents *sharp* to Equal Temperament, so it sounds nearly a quarter-tone sharp to the Bb in (1).

Next, set History to 4 and play this pattern over and over again: C4-Bb5-D4-Bb5; in this case the Bb should always sound the same because the fundamental (60.0) does not change to D4 mid-pattern. Play with this and other settings while monitoring the “current fundamental” and “note” values to learn more about how it is working.

#### Adaptive Tuning

With Adaptive, the Anchor scale menus are irrelevant; instead of using the anchor scale, the next adapted note will now become the new “anchor,” which will continuously change while playing. Set History back to 1 and play an ascending scale; you should see that the “current fundamental” gets reset with every note played (as before) and that its value is always the same as the “note” tuning.

This is where things can get strange and fun\! Play this pattern over and over again:

||: C4-D4-E4 :||

Why does the pitch drift up? Every note is being tuned with the *prior* note as the fundamental. We begin with two whole steps, each tuned as the *first* whole step in a Just scale (interval \= 2.039, slightly larger than two ET  half steps), followed by a descending major-third, also tuned as it would be in a Just scale (interval \= \-3.863, so slightly *smaller* than four Equal Tempered half-steps). The two just-tuned whole-steps yield a major third that is *larger* than the just tuned major-third, so the whole system begins to drift upwards. 

Try this pattern, and hear how the pitch drifts down:

	||: E4-D4-C4 :||

If the “invert” toggle is checked, the downward drift should move at the same pace as the upward drift from the prior example, because Tuning will consider both ascending and descending intervals as the same (a whole-step is a whole step, whether going up or down). But with “invert” unchecked, the second example will drift down more quickly than the first. This is because, in short, the downward Just-tuned whole step is treated like the minor-7th of the Just scale, which is a much bigger whole step than the upward whole step. For a temperament with some slight differences, try the Duodene scale. Feel free to refer to the [Appendix](#appendix) at the end of this manual for how each pre-programmed bitKlavier interval is tuned. 

To further explore the Adaptive Tuning feature, load Example Gallery 17, “Tuning 2.” Instructions for how to begin using the Adaptive Tuning settings are written directly into the Gallery. Adjust the maximum number of pitches, time threshold, and adaptive temperament, each of which helps to determine how and when the Tuning preparation will shift based on Keymap input. Also, check out the *Mikroetude* called *Didymus,* which uses Resets to manually anchor the Adaptive Tuning.

Adaptive tuning is a wide-open field of study, and these two approaches (Adaptive & Adaptive Anchored) are meant to be more exploratory than “solutions” that always yield some kind of optimal or neutral tuning. While Adaptive Tuning systems may be used to create consistent optimal tunings, systems with their own idiosyncrasies create valuable compositional opportunities, and these Adaptive Tunings can be used to satisfy either goal. We are currently exploring a range of richer systems, including the spring tuning system described next.

#### Spring Tuning

Some years ago, John de Laubenfels proposed an intriguing system for optimizing the tuning of sonorities. This system is detailed in William Sethares’ book [*Tuning Timbre Spectrum Scale*](http://sethares.engr.wisc.edu/ttss.html)*,* but was never to our knowledge fully implemented (though recently [Stange, et al](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04338.pdf). created a similar system). Our implementation is largely inspired by de Laubenfels, though is not identical, and is also different in key ways from Stange’s system, discussion of which is beyond the scope of this manual.

As with the other adaptive systems, in your Piano, Keymap must be connected to Tuning *as well as* Direct, so that Tuning knows what notes to activate in the spring system. 

##### Basic Functionality

The key concept is that intervals are modeled by virtual springs with rest lengths determined by a chosen tuning system (usually just). So, a major third would typically have a rest spring length of 386 cents, a perfect fifth a rest length of 702 cents, and so on. When more than two notes are played, springs of the appropriate length are connected between them all, and they pull on one another until they reach a condition where each is minimally stretched or compressed, optimizing the tuning. The relative strengths of the various intervals can be set, so, say, major third springs are stronger than, say, perfect fifth springs, and the system will respond accordingly.

![][image66]

##### Tether Anchors

In addition, a background set of “anchor notes” (represented by the spiral) is connected to active notes via another set of springs, which help prevent the system from drifting. In the image above, the anchor scale is equal tempered (as set by the top-most menu) and the interval scale that sets the default lengths of the interval springs is just (as set by the menu just below the anchor scale menu). The relative strengths of the springs to the anchor notes can also be set, allowing some pitches to be favored and others to be totally unmoored, if desired; in the above image, all the interval and anchor springs are set to equal strengths of 0.5, slightly distorting the tuning of the intervals, while in the following image only the C anchor spring is “on,” so the triad is more perfectly tuned:

![][image67]

##### Stiffness, Rate, and Drag

The overall *stiffness* of the interval and anchor springs affects the dynamics of the system, causing the springs to vibrate more or less quickly, and the *drag* models a kind of friction in the system (imagine the notes being dragged through molasses), damping the spring oscillations. Finally, the *rate* (in Hz) determines how often the spring model runs. All four of these parameters can be adjusted to create a wide range of different responses, from slowly oscillating systems to almost inaudible and instantaneous tunings. 

##### Interval Scale and Fundamental

One of the more complex components of this system is the *interval scale fundamental:*

![][image68]

When set to “none,” the behavior is as described so far, where the resting length for a spring is set only with regards to the interval between its two pitches. So, for example, every M2nd spring will be set to 204c when using the just scale, which has a 9/8 M2nd between the root and M2nd:

| Interval | U | m2 | M2 | m3 | M3 | P4 | a4/d5 | P5 | m6 | M6 | m7 | M7 |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Ratio | **1/1** | **16/15** | **9/8** | **6/5** | **5/4** | **4/3** | **7/5** | **3/2** | **8/5** | **5/3** | **7/4** | **15/8** |
| Length (cents) | **0** | **111** | **204** | **315** | **386** | **498** | **582** | **702** | **813** | **884** | **968** | **1088** |

In this case, if you play a C-D-E trichord, the D will be squeezed by its springs on either side, and it will in turn push the C-E M3rd a bit wide. Here is the M3rd by itself:

![][image69]

And now with the D inserted between:

![][image70]

If we set the interval scale fundamental to C, however, the D-E M2nd will use the 10/9 ratio (386 \- 204 \= 182c, from the table above) of that just scale (which is the ratio between the major 2nd and 3rd in that scale; 9/8 \* 10/9 \= 5/4), so all the springs will naturally sit at their rest lengths:

![][image71]

Setting the fundamental to “lowest” will use the lowest sounding note for the fundamental, and “highest” the highest sounding note, while “last” will use the last played note; all can yield interesting behaviors with compositional possibilities. 

Another example: try playing a C4 dominant 7th chord using “last” as the interval scale fundamental (and setting the anchor spring strengths to zero for the E4, G4 and Bb4), and compare the sound of the chord when arpeggiating it upwards vs downwards; can you figure out why these sound different?

Here’s what it should look like after playing the chord ascending:  
![][image72]

And descending:  
![][image73]

##### Fundamental Weights and Other Weights

These two knobs set how strong the tether springs are for the fundamental vs all the other pitches. For instance, if the fundamental is C, then C’s will have tether springs with a weight set by “FUND WEIGHTS” while all other pitches will have weights set by “OTHER WEIGHTS.” This can be useful in cases where you want to ground sonorities to particular pitches, as in this example, where the fundamental is weighted much more strongly, so the CE third results in a C that is exactly at the tether location (0c offset) and the E is offset:

![][image74]

If we make the weights equal, the offsets from the background spiral will equal out:

![][image75]

##### Fundamental “F” vs Local Lengths

Notice the addition of the yellow F squares by each interval spring; these are toggles that allow you to decide whether to use the moving fundamental as a reference for setting the spring length, or whether to revert to the more “local” approach described earlier, as in “none” mode. 

Why do this? bitKlavier’s movable fundamental allows us to retain some of the richness of the non-unique interval sizes (the M2, for instance) in a coherent fashion. But, one paradoxical consequence of this is that after notes have been added or subtracted from a sonority and the springs have stopped oscillating, they will all be at their rest lengths; this is essentially tautological, since using the spring length table this way guarantees that all spring lengths will be compatible, but not unique—we might have, for instance, two different spring lengths for the perfect 5th, one for the familiar 3:2 ratio, and another for a “wolf” interval (40:27 between D and A in Table 1, when the fundamental is C), or the two different M2nds as already described.

For instance, with C as the interval fundamental and all intervals using the fundamental (“F”) for choosing their spring lengths, a D-A fifth will be quite compressed and out-of-tune sounding, because of the way that particular 5th is funding in C-just:

![][image76]

But when using the local spring length (ignoring the fundamentals), that fifth ends up being a perfect 3:2, because the system uses the first fifth it encounters in the just scale:

![][image77]

##### Individual Interval Weighting

We might also want to weigh some intervals more heavily than others. For instance, we might care about perfect 5ths being closer to pure than, say, major 6ths. Consider this sonority, CDGA, with two fifths framed by a major 6th:

![][image78]

With all the intervals weighted equally, the DA fifth ends up quite compressed (691 cents) because of the small CA 6th. If we increase the weight of the perfect 5th, that DA fifth approaches nearly perfect (700 cents):

![][image79]

while expanding the DA 6th slightly to 894 cents. 

##### Automatic Fundamental Finding

The *highest, lowest,* and *last* modes beg the question: can’t bitKlavier just figure out what an ideal fundamental would be to tune whatever sonority is play “as just as possible?” Of course, that is a qualitative question, but for the examples considered so far (a stack of two whole-steps, the dominant 7th chord) it’s a reasonable one. In *automatic* fundamental mode (new as of v2.4), bitKlavier looks at the sounding notes and tries to determine whether they suggest a particular overtone series, inspired in part by the psychoacoustic phenomenon of the “missing fundamental.” Below, we see the overtone series based on C, and then its first few intervals, in complementary octave pairings, so the P5/P4, the M3/m6, and the m3/M6. The *automatic* algorithm works down from the top of whatever chord is sounding looking for these intervals; if it finds any of these intervals, it returns a fundamental of C. It prioritizes 5ths and 4ths over the M3/m6, and similarly the M3/m6 over the m3/M6, in the event that different intervals suggest different fundamentals, and by working from the top down, it prioritizes lower register voices; imagine a stack of perfect fifths, and the bottom fifth would determine what the fundamental is. If none of these intervals are found, then it leaves the fundamental unchanged.

![][image80]

This simple algorithm is inexpensive to calculate, even when many notes are sounding, and it yields predictable and intuitive results; the C-D-E trichord yields a C fundamental, as does a C dominant 7th chord, and so on.

Learn more about all this in our Computer Journal Paper:

* “[Tuning Playfully: Composed and Adaptive Tunings in bitKlavier](https://manyarrowsmusic.com/papers/Tuning_Playfully_with_bitKlavier.comj_a_00519.pdf).” Dan Trueman, Aatish Bhatia, Michael Mulshine, and Theo Trevisan. Computer Music Journal, Vol. 43, Nos. 2-3 (2019)

### Scala Import

Drag/drop [Scala](https://www.huygens-fokker.org/scala/) SCL and KBM files onto the bitKlavier Scala and KBM text windows to import them into bitKlavier:

![][image81]

When you import a SCL file and then press “map Scala to internal tuning,” bitKlavier will generate a representation of that tuning in its own interface. If the tuning uses more or less than twelve keys (as in the above example, Bohlen Pierce tuning), it will generate an Absolute tuning, adjusting each key as needed:

![][image82]

When you import a 12-note tuning system, bitKlavier will generate a Custom one-octave tuning:  
![][image83]

Note that if you want to use the new Custom tuning that this “map” creates, switch back to “static” mode from “Scala KBM” mode, otherwise bitKlavier will continue to just use whatever is in the SCL/KBM text windows. 

KBM files allow SCL files to be mapped in specific ways to the keyboard, and are of particular use for non-12-note systems (like the Bohlen-Pierce example above). See the Scala website for [documentation of the KBM format](https://www.huygens-fokker.org/scala/help.htm#mappings).

***SIDEBAR:***   
We’ve been asked why we didn’t support Scala earlier. One reason is that I did not find that I needed Scala; every tuning system is unique, and has a history and motivation, and each one takes time to get to know. The original bitKlavier had only a few tuning systems, ones that I knew well, trained my ears on, and used in various compositions. These were later expanded with a number of historical tunings from Western European (and more recent) traditions. See [Carey Beebe’s wonderful website](http://www.hpschd.nu/index.html?nav/nav-4.html&t/welcome.html&http://www.hpschd.nu/tech/tmp/spiral.html) for information about the histories of all of these tunings, and for recipes for how to tune an instrument with each of them; if you’d like to try your hand actually *doing* these tunings by ear, you can with a virtual harpsichord tuning application I made a few years ago, called *bitTemper*: [manual](http://manyarrowsmusic.com/bitKlavier/bitSuite_Manual.pdf), [max-patches](http://manyarrowsmusic.com//bitKlavier/bitDyadStringTemper_src.zip). 

To be honest, I found the enormous catalog of Scala tunings to be overwhelming, and the tunings often felt detached from their roots, so if I wanted to explore a particular tuning, I would learn about it and create it by hand in bitKlavier, which in and of itself helped me get to know it. In spite of this, we’ve gone ahead now and integrated Scala import, just so bitKlavier can play a bit more nicely with the rest of the tuning-aware world, but my own reservations remain. If you are interested in learning more about these systems, or others, I recommend exploring [Leimma and Apotome](https://isartum.net), created by Khyam Allami and Counterpoint.  
—Dan

Special thanks to the folks from [Surge Synth Team and their Tuning Library](https://github.com/surge-synthesizer/tuning-library), which made this possible\! Their [Tuning Workbench Synth](https://surge-synth-team.org/tuning-workbench-synth/) is a great tool for creating SCL/KBM files, by the way.

### MTS-ESP (Tuning preparation)

#### What it is

[MTS-ESP](https://github.com/ODDSound/MTS-ESP) is a system that lets one plugin broadcast a tuning to every other MTS-ESP-aware plugin running in your DAW (or on your computer, in the case of the standalone). bitKlavier can act as the **MTS-ESP master**: any Tuning preparation can publish its tuning so that other microtonal-capable instruments and effects automatically follow bitKlavier's tuning — in real time, including while notes are sustaining.

bitKlavier supports **both directions**:

- **Master / publishing** — a Tuning broadcasts its tuning to other plugins (described below).  
- **Client / receive** — a Tuning takes its tuning *from* another MTS-ESP master (see "Receiving a tuning (MTS-ESP Client)" at the end).

#### How to use it

1. Open any Tuning preparation. At the top-left of the popup, next to the close (✕) button, you'll see a **Set MTS-ESP Master** button and a status label.  
2. Click **Set MTS-ESP Master**. bitKlavier claims the MTS-ESP master role and begins publishing this Tuning. The button changes to **MTS-ESP Master: ON**.  
3. Open any MTS-ESP-aware client plugin in your session — it will pick up bitKlavier's tuning automatically.  
4. Click the button again to turn it off and release the master role.

**Only one Tuning can be the MTS-ESP master at a time.** Selecting a different Tuning as master automatically deselects the previous one — there is a single master per bitKlavier instance/gallery, not a per-Tuning switch.

Whatever the selected Tuning does, the clients follow. With **Spring** or **Adaptive** tunings, the published tuning updates continuously as the tuning evolves, so connected clients bend along with bitKlavier during sustained notes.

#### Status messages

The label to the right of the button tells you what's happening:

| Message | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| `off` | No Tuning is selected as master. |
| `MTS-ESP Master: ON` / `Publishing (N clients)` | This Tuning is the master and is broadcasting. `N` is how many MTS-ESP clients are currently connected (it can be 0 — that just means nothing is listening yet). |
| `another Tuning is master` | A *different* Tuning in this gallery is the master. Click this one's button to take over. |
| `Blocked - another MTS-ESP master is running` | Another application or plugin already owns the MTS-ESP master role. bitKlavier won't take it from them. (See "If it's blocked" below.) |
| `MTS-ESP library not installed` | The MTS-ESP system library isn't installed on this computer, so master mode can't run. Install it (it ships with bitKlavier) and try again. |
| `disabled in build` | This build of bitKlavier was compiled without MTS-ESP support. |

#### If it's blocked

If you click **Set MTS-ESP Master** and bitKlavier reports it's blocked *but you know nothing else is acting as master*, this is usually **stale state** left behind by a plugin that crashed or was force-quit without releasing MTS-ESP. bitKlavier will offer a dialog:

**MTS-ESP master unavailable** — … you can reinitialize MTS-ESP and take over. **\[Reinitialize & take over\]** **\[Cancel\]**

Choosing **Reinitialize & take over** clears the orphaned state and makes bitKlavier the master. Only do this if you're certain no other app is genuinely acting as the MTS-ESP master, since it resets MTS-ESP for the whole system.

#### Saving, loading, and switching

- The master selection is **saved with your gallery**. Reopening a gallery restores it and bitKlavier attempts to become master again.  
- If the saved master Tuning no longer exists (e.g. it was deleted), the selection is simply cleared on load.  
- Deleting the Tuning that is currently the master turns MTS-ESP master off.  
- Switching the active piano does **not** interrupt publishing — the selected master keeps broadcasting regardless of which piano is active.  
- bitKlavier releases the MTS-ESP master role automatically when you close the plugin or quit the app.

#### Receiving a tuning (MTS-ESP Client)

A Tuning preparation can also *follow* an external MTS-ESP master instead of generating its own tuning:

1. Open the Tuning preparation and set its **Tuning Type** menu to **MTS Client**.  
2. The Tuning's internal controls hide — its pitches now come from whatever MTS-ESP master is running (another plugin, or another bitKlavier). The spiral display shows the received tuning.  
3. If no master is connected, the Tuning falls back to standard 12-TET until one appears.

Notes:

- This is **per Tuning** — different Tunings can independently follow the master or use their own tunings, and several can be clients at once.  
- Receive mode tracks the master in real time, including while notes sustain.  
- A Tuning can be a client *or* a master, not both meaningfully at once.

#### Limitations

- **One master per bitKlavier instance/gallery.**  
- **One master per system** — this is an MTS-ESP rule, not a bitKlavier one. If you run two bitKlavier instances (or another master plugin), only one can hold the role; the others show `Blocked`.  
- Other plugins must themselves support MTS-ESP to follow bitKlavier's tuning.  
- The MTS-ESP system library must be installed (it ships with bitKlavier's installer).

| Tempo |
| :---- |

### What is it?

The Tempo preparation provides control to any connected Synchronic or Blendronic preparation in bitKlavier. There are two Tempo settings, **Constant Tempo** and **Adaptive Tempo**. If using multiple Synchronic/Blendronic preparations, a single Tempo preparation can control all of them, or each preparation could use its own individual Tempo preparation. Tempo only controls the preparations to which it is connected. 

### How to make a Tempo Preparation

To add a Tempo preparation to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Tempo.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut ‘m,’ and the Tempo will appear in the Construction site. Double-click on the Tempo preparation, and you’ll see the pop-up window displayed below. By default, it is in “Constant Tempo” mode, but selecting different modes will display different parameters.

![][image84]  
*Parameters in Constant Tempo mode & Host Tempo mode*

### ![][image85]

*Parameters in Adaptive \- Time Between Notes mode & Adaptive \- Sustain Time mode*

### Navigating the Tempo Preparation

#### Constant Tempo Parameters

***Tempo:*** controls metronome values from 40.0 to 208.0 bpm. Higher or lower positive values can be achieved by control-clicking on the knob and typing in the desired value. The knob will rescale to have this value as the maximum/minimum.

***Subdivisions:*** sets how many pulses will be sent per “beat” as set by the “tempo” knob; for instance, when subdivisions \= 4, and the tempo \= 120, this will be interpreted as pulses at 480bpm; this should allow for more intuitive tempo settings, especially when working within a DAW. 

#### Adaptive Tempo Parameters

Adaptive Tempo determines the pace of a Synchronic sequence by taking a running average of the time between user-played notes. Adaptive Tempo will only work if it is attached to a Synchronic preparation *and* a Keymap preparation, because the input from the Keymap provides information that adapts the tempo to your playing. 

**History**: number of MIDI strokes bitKlavier is retroactively counting to find the average time

**Subdivisions**: tempo multiplier by interpreting the history. If you play 4 quarter notes and subdivision is set to 2, it doubles the tempo by basing the current tempo value on four eighth notes. Values less than 1 are also possible, to create slower tempi.

***Time Window Min/Max:*** tells Tempo to ignore notes above or below a certain length and spacing

#### Host Tempo

When using bitKlavier as a plugin, choosing “Host Tempo” will enable bitKlavier to follow tempo changes of the host directly.

| MIDI Filter |
| :---- |

### What is it?

The MIDI Filter preparation allows a user to choose which types of MIDI messages get sent to preparations. This preparation is meant to be situated between a Keymap preparation and some other preparation. It receives MIDI messages from the Keymap, but will only pass the MIDI messages along to the other preparation if it corresponds to the MIDI Filter option applied by the user (e.g. ascending notes only).

### How to make a Reset Preparation

To add a MIDI Filter preparation to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “MIDI Filter.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut SHIFT \+ ‘f,’ and the MIDI Filter will appear in the Construction site. Double-click on the MIDI Filter preparation, and you’ll see the pop-up window displayed below.

![][image86]

### MIDI Target Options

Most of the MIDI Target options are self-explanatory…

- ***all notes off\!***  
- ***toggle noteOn/Off***  
- ***ignore noteOn***  
- ***ignore noteOff***  
- ***invert noteOn/Off***  
- ***ignore sustain pedal***  
- ***treat sustain pedal like sostenuto pedal***  
- ***treat keys like sustain pedal***  
- ***treat keys like sostenuto pedal***  
- ***ascending notes only***  
- ***descending notes only***  
- ***repeated notes only***

Give them a try to see how they work.

| MIDI Target |
| :---- |

### What does MIDI Target do?

A MIDI Target allows a user to define how certain types of MIDI messages (NoteOn, NoteOff, or both) will alter the behavior of an attached preparation. The MIDI Target will receive MIDI messages from the attached Keymap preparation, determine if any of those messages should have an effect on the behavior of the attached preparation, and then trigger that behavior if so.

The MIDI Target is a dynamic preparation that allows us to target events in the preparations that it’s connected to. It will always take a Keymap as input and can be connected to the following preparations: Direct, Blendronic, Nostalgic, Resonance, Synchronic, Tempo, or Tuning. Depending on the preparation that it is attached to, the options in its pop-up window will change. This means that a MIDI Target can be connected to multiple preparations of the same type but not preparations of different types. 

### How to make a MIDI Target Preparation

To add a MIDI Target preparation to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “MIDI Target.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut SHIFT \+ ‘t,’ and the MIDI Target will appear in the Construction site. Since it doesn’t have any functionality on its own, double-clicking on this preparation will display a blank pop-up window. Once it is attached to another preparation, it will populate with different options. The gallery below depicts all of the preparation types that a MIDI Target can be attached to. It also demonstrates that a MIDI Target can be connected to multiple preparations of the same type.

![][image87]

### Navigating the MIDI Target Preparation

The following sections will examine the options available in MIDI Target when it is attached to different preparation types. Preparations are ordered by increasing number of parameters; starting with Direct, which has two available actions, and ending with Synchronic, which has seven available actions.

In every case, MIDI Target displays a column of action buttons on the left and a column of dropdown menus on the right. To select which type of behavior the preparation will target, a user must click the action button so that it turns purple. To select which type of MIDI message will trigger the behavior, a user will select one of the three options listed in the dropdown menu: NoteOn, NoteOff, and Both (NoteOn and NoteOff). 

By default, action buttons are turned off, the Default Behavior dropdowns are set to Both, and the remaining dropdown menus are set to NoteOn.

***Default Behavior:*** Every preparation that can be connected to a MIDI Target (except for Blendronic) has a *Default Behavior* option. This allows the connected preparation to treat MIDI messages as it normally would. This is helpful for when a user might want a certain key to trigger some behavior while also being processed normally.

***Reset Mods:*** Every preparation that can be connected to a MIDI Target has a *Reset Mods* option. When this is triggered, ALL of the modifications that have been triggered by Mods attached to that preparation will be reset to their saved values; this is equivalent to attaching a Reset preparation to every Mod preparation and triggering it.

#### Direct

***Default Behavior:*** treats MIDI messages as it normally would  
***Reset Mods:*** resets modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details)

#### Nostalgic 

***Default Behavior:*** treats MIDI messages as it normally would (see above for more details)  
***Clear:*** clear the ongoing Nostalgic waves  
***Reset Mods:*** resets modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details)

#### Tuning

***Default Behavior:*** treats MIDI messages as it normally would (see above for more details)  
***Reset Mods:*** resets modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details)  
***Reset:*** triggers an adaptive reset; updates the adaptive fundamental value

#### Tempo

***Default Behavior:*** treats MIDI messages as it normally would (see above for more details)  
***Reset Mods:*** resets continuous modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details)  
***Reset:*** triggers an adaptive reset

#### Resonance

***Default Behavior:*** treats MIDI messages as it normally would (see above for more details)  
***Ring Strings:*** rings strings existing in the resonant structure  
***Add/Remove String:*** notes will be added/removed to the resonant structure, but they won’t actually ring the resonances unless “ring strings” is also toggled on  
***Reset Mods:*** resets modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details)

***Notes:***  
With ***Add/Remove String***, notes will be added to or removed from the resonant structure, but they won’t actually *ring* the resonances unless ***Ring Strings*** is also toggled on. This allows a user to set sympathetic strings with one keyboard and then actually ring those resonant strings with another keyboard. This is reminiscent of instruments like the Hardanger fiddle or the viola d’amore: they have static, pre-tuned sympathetic strings, and then separate strings that are bowed, which in turn “ring” the sympathetic strings. This separation of targeting decouples how the resonant structure is built, and how it is activated. 

#### Blendronic

***Pattern Sync:*** restarts the patterns (Beat Lengths, Delay Lengths, etc…) on the next beat; the pulse itself is NOT reset.  
***Beat Sync:*** the pulse is reset, but the patterns are not.   
***Clear:*** clear the delays.  
***Pause/Play:*** pause playback and without changing the contents of the delay-line; then play will restart it, as it was before pause.  
***Open/Close Input:*** stops and starts “recording” into the delay line; it will still playback, it just won’t add anything more to the delay..  
***Open/Close Output:*** when closed, will continue to “record” into the delay line, but nothing will be played back until it is opened again.  
***Reset Mods:*** resets modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details)

#### Synchronic

***Default Behavior:*** treats MIDI messages as it normally would (see above for more details)  
***Pattern Sync:*** restarts the patterns (Accents, Transpositions, etc…) on the next beat; the pulse itself is NOT reset.  
***Beat Sync:*** the pulse is reset, but the patterns are not. The normal Synchronic behavior is for both of these to be reset, so this allows them to be decoupled.  
***Add Notes:*** played notes are added to the cluster without resetting the patterns or pulse.  
***Clear:*** clear all ongoing clusters/pulses.  
***Pause/Play:*** pause all clusters if they are playing, or restart playing them if they are paused.  
***Reset Mods:*** resets modifications attached to the preparation (see above for more details).

| Modifications |
| :---- |

### What is it?

Modifications are a powerful set of tools for changing the bitKlavier settings dynamically, triggered directly from the performance of the player. For instance, a particular key could be set to change the tuning system, and another could be set to fade out the Blendrónic preparation. A third key could be set to cause a Reverberator level to oscillate slowly, while another could be set to instantly change the accent pattern in Synchronic. All of this done by the player without lifting their hands from the keyboard.

### How to set up a Modification?

Create a Modification (‘c’ or choose from the Preparation menu), drag/drop it on top of the preparation you want to modify to create a referential connection, and then connect a Keymap to the Modification and set which key(s) in the Keymap that you want to trigger the modification. Here is a simple Mod connected to Tuning.

![][image88]

If you want to remove the referential connection to a preparation, simply drag the Mod on top of the preparation again. 

To set the specific of the modification, double-click on the preparation (Tuning, in this example), which will open both the Tuning and the Modification popup windows:

![][image89]

### Value Change Modification

At the top right, click “add modification” and choose (for instance) Value Change, and then drag that Value Change (using its selection box at its top left) on top of the parameter you want to modify:

![][image90]

Here, the Value Change has been connected to the Semitone Width parameter. Drag on the little knob about the connected parameter to set the target value for the modification. Then, press the key you selected to trigger this modification to actually change the value to the target:

![][image91]

The new value will be visible in the green sleeve and also in a popup display directly to the right of the parameter when you hover over it.

Control-click on a knob to access a set of options for manipulation the modification. 

##### Time and Curve knobs

The “time” knob sets how long to take to make the full modification; this will be a sample-accurate ramp change. The “curve” knob makes that ramp non-linear; smaller values (\<1.0) will cause the change to happen more quickly and the beginning of the ramp and then slow down, whereas values greater than 1.0 will cause the change to happen more slowly at the beginning and more quickly at the end.

##### Toggle Mode

If toggle mode is selected, then re-triggering the modification will cause it to reset to its saved value.

### Oscillating Change

This is for LFO (Low Frequency Oscillator) modifications. Drag one of these on a parameter and set the oscillation range with the small modulation amount knob above the parameter, and then trigger the mod with your selected key to set the parameter in motion.

By default, these will only activate when the Mod is triggered by a noteOn message, and will stop when the corresponding noteOff message is received. It is possible to toggle it on and off with successive noteOn messages by using a MIDIFilter preparation in “toggle noteOn/Off” mode:

![][image92]

##### Auto mode

Alternatively, you can turn on “auto” mode and the parameter will oscillate automatically, without any keyboard control. 

##### Oscillator Types

There are a range of standard LFO types available in the pulldown menu, including sine, square, sawtooth up, sawtooth down, triangle, and randeom

### State Modifications

State modifications are for parameters that are not continuous, or are complex state parameters with many values. 

#### Menu State Modification

A common state modification is simply to change the value of a menu. In this case, we are using a state modification to change the fundamental of a tuning system:

![][image93]

Click on the green box to choose the target menu item you want the modification to go to.

#### Keyboard Modifications

We could also have the state of the tuning changed:

![][image94]

Here, after clicking on the modification box directly below the keyboard, we can see the “MODIFIED” state we are aiming for.

#### Complex State Modifications

We might want to change the accent pattern in the Synchronic preparation:

![][image95]

We click on the green selection box, after making the connection (dragging the State Change on top of the Accents slider), to create our target modification:

![][image96]

Triggering that modification will cause the actual values to change to the values we have set in “MODIFIED.”

### Multiple Simultaneous Mods

It is possible to connect a single modification to multiple parameters, and also possible to connect multiple Modification preparations to a single preparation parameter, and in general they will sum. If you have times set for ramps, and trigger new mods while a ramp is still running, they will both continue to aim for their targets, so you will likely not end up at either’s target\! This can be fun if confusing. Using Reset (below) can help make the behavior cleaner. 

| Reset |
| :---- |

***What does Reset do?***  
Whenever Reset is triggered, it will instantly revert connected modifications to their initial settings.

***How to make a Reset Preparation***  
To add a Reset preparation to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Reset.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut ‘\\,’ and the Reset will appear in the Construction site. 

Since the behavior of this preparation doesn’t require any parameter changes from a user,  double-clicking on the Reset preparation will not display a pop-up window like the other preparations.

***An Example of the Reset Preparation***  
An example of how the Reset preparation can be used in a bitKlavier composition is shown below in the gallery for Dan’s piece “Marbles.” The Keymap attached to the Reset preparation only passes MIDI messages when the C7 key is played. This means that when a user plays C7, the Reset preparation will be triggered, setting the attached modification preparation to its right to its default settings.

![][image97]

Resets via MIDI Target are also possible; see the [MIDI Target section](#midi-target).

| Piano Switch |
| :---- |

### What does Piano Switch do?

The Piano Switch preparation allows a user to move through different Pianos within the same Gallery by simply using Keymap input. This could be used mid-performance to switch between movements, or while experimenting in bitKlavier with two different Piano presets.

### How to make a Piano Switch Preparation

To add a Piano Switch preparation to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Piano Switch.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut ‘p,’ and the Piano Switch will appear in the Construction site.

Since this preparation requires that the user only specifies one parameter \- which piano should be loaded upon Keymap input \- it doesn’t need an entire pop-up window like the other preparations. Instead of double-clicking on the Piano Switch, simply click on the 3 text (by default, “---”) and select the desired piano.

### An Example of the Piano Switch Preparation

bitKlavier galleries can contain several pianos, as is the case with Dan’s composition “Inside Out.” The image below depicts the gallery for this piece as well as the many pianos that exist within it, which can be accessed by the Piano Menu.

![][image98]

The Keymap attached to the Piano Switch preparation is set to only send messages when a particular G\# (highlighted on the bottom keyboard) is played. When a user plays that note, the Piano Switch will change from the current piano (displayed in the Menu Bar under “Piano” to be “0. Only Hammers”) to the selected piano, which is “1. Hammers+Resonance.”

In this piece, a user traverses through different pianos sequentially. When piano “1. Hammers+Resonance” loads, the gallery appears as below. Piano 1 similarly has a Piano Switch preparation, but this time it will switch to Piano 2 when the chosen note is played.

![][image99] 

Note that a Piano Switch is not a global control and will only exist in the Piano in which it is created.

| Comment |
| :---- |

### What is a Comment?

Nothing fancy here\! The Comment preparation is simply a way to add a comment to your Gallery so that a user can add notes, instructions, or any other text.

### How to make a Comment

To add a Comment to your Gallery, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Comment.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut ‘/,’ and a Comment will appear in the Construction site.

### How to use a Comment

Upon its creation, a Comment will prompt a user to “double-click to type.” Double-clicking opens up a text box where any notes can be added. When done typing, simply click outside of the Comment box, and the text will be neatly displayed within a box that can be moved and resized.

### Format Customization

Comment also allows for format customization. After double-clicking on the Comment, control-clicking will display the following menu:

![][image100]

The menu includes functionality for cutting, copying, pasting, deleting, and selecting all text. Undo allows a user to revert their most recent change. Text can be horizontally aligned to the left, right, or center, and it can be vertically aligned to the top, middle, or bottom. Text can be bolded, italicized, and colored. Available colors include: white, yellow, cyan, light green, coral, orange, red, blue, and pink. The background of the Comment can be: gray (default), black, or transparent.

At the bottom of the Comment menu are notes for how a user can use inline text to format their comment. By surrounding a piece of text by one asterisk (\*like so\*), the text will be italicized. Two asterisks on either side bolds the text. By stating the color in brackets on either side of the text ({red} like so {/red}, notice the slash in the closing set of brackets), the text can be colored to one of the options stated above. Any text preceded with one, two, or three pound (\#) symbols and followed by a new line (pressing enter/return) will be formatted as a heading, where more pound symbols makes the heading smaller. Like many text editors, a bulleted list can be created by adding a dash (-) or asterisk (\*) to the start of each line and an ordered list can be created by adding a number to the start of each line. 

![][image101]![][image102]

| Compressor |
| :---- |

### What is it?

A compressor allows users to control the dynamics to their sound directly in bitKlavier. Users might choose to use the compressor to get a more consistent volume level or to alter the tone completely. Note that the compressor must be powered on by pressing the power button near the top left; it is off by default. You might find that a signal is unpredictable \- compressor allows you to adjust the signal to keep it from causing distortion or getting unexpectedly too loud

### How to make a Compressor Preparation

There is both the global Compressor, which affects all preparations in the Construction Site, and Compressors as individual preparations, which can be attached to specific preparations. To access the global Compressor, click the Compressor button in the lower right-hand corner, between the keyboard and gain meter and between the Equalizer and Reverberator buttons.

To add a Compressor preparation to the Construction Site, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Compressor.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut SHIFT \+ ‘c,’ and the Compressor will appear in the Construction site. Double-click on the Compressor preparation, and you’ll see the pop-up window displayed below.

![][image103]

### Compressor Parameters

**Attack and Release**  
The attack and release parameters  determine the time it takes for the compressor to engage gain reduction and return to normal volume levels after the signal goes below the threshold value. Double-clicking on the knob returns them to their default values (5.0ms and 20ms). 

**Threshold, Ratio, and Knee**  
Threshold determines the signal volume needed to engage the compressor. Ratio determines the amount of gain reduction applied when the compressor is fully engaged. Knee determines the shape of compression after it has been engaged as it moves to the full ratio. A lower value means it will reach peak compression quicker. Double-clicking returns the slider returns them to their defaults (0.0dBFS, 1:1, 0.0)

| Equalizer |
| :---- |

### What is it?

A parametric equalizer allows users to fine tune the sound spectrum of their custom Galleries by emphasizing or de-emphasizing specific bands of frequencies. Users might choose to alter the strength of certain bands of frequencies in order to better suit their room, speaker system, or audio equipment, or to re-envision entirely the sound of a custom Gallery. Parameter selections will be saved when a user chooses to “save” their custom Gallery.  Helpful for adjusting based on the room

### How to make an Equalizer Preparation

There is both the global Equalizer, which affects all preparations in the Construction Site, and Equalizers as individual preparations, which can be attached to specific preparations. To access the global Equalizer, click the Equalizer button in the lower right-hand corner, between the keyboard and gain meter and above the Compressor button.

To add an Equalizer preparation to the Construction Site, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Equalizer.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut SHIFT \+ ‘e,’ and the Equalizer will appear in the Construction site. Double-click on the Equalizer preparation, and you’ll see the pop-up window displayed below.

![][image104]

### Equalizer Parameters

**Graphic Display** \- a visualization of how the equalizer’s parameters affect the frequency spectrum, from 20Hz to 20,000Hz. When the equalizer is powered off, the display will appear as a flat line.

![][image105]

**Cut Filter Parameters** \- The left-most column in the EQ contains the parameters for a low cut (high pass) filter, and the right-most column contains the parameters for a high cut (low pass) filter. Both of these cut filters use the same parameters: frequency and slope. To alter these parameters, make sure the equalizer is powered on then click the image at the top of the column to activate the filter. When a filter is on, the image will be white and will otherwise be grayed out. The frequency parameter of the low-cut filter controls the highest frequency (or in the case of the high cut filter, the lowest frequency) that the filter will not attenuate. The slope parameter affects how drastically the filter attenuates frequencies just below (or in the case of the high cut filter, just above) the cutoff frequency. A higher slope corresponds to more drastic attenuation just beyond the cutoff frequency. Try changing the frequency and slope values while glancing at the graphic display to get a feel for how these parameters affect the frequency spectrum.

**![][image106]![][image107]**

**Peak Filter Parameters** \- the three peak filters \- the columns between the cut filters \- have their own parameters which behave differently than the cut filters. To alter these parameters, first select one of the peak filters using the three middle peak filter selection buttons. Each of the peak filters works by attenuating or boosting frequencies in the shape of a peak (or valley)—frequencies nearest the center are most strongly affected and frequencies far from the center are less strongly affected. The frequency parameter controls the frequency around which the peak centers. The gain controls how much the peak rises or sinks. 0db corresponds to no change, while a positive db indicates a boost (with higher numbers being a more significant boost) and a negative db indicates a cut (with lower numbers being a more significant attenuation). Quality relates to the bandwidth of the filter—the slope of the peak. A higher quality indicates a steeper slope, while a lower quality indicates a gentler slope. Adjust these sliders while glancing at the graphic display to get a feel for how changing these parameters affects the frequency spectrum.

![][image108]

**Reset and Bypass** \- the currently selected filter can be reset to its default values. It can also be temporarily bypassed to hear the effects of the filter compared with the unfiltered sound. Likewise, the entire equalizer can be reset to its default values. It can also be bypassed to temporarily audition the unaffected sound of the current Gallery. When this option is selected, the graphic display will appear greyed out.

| Reverberator |
| :---- |

### What is it?

The reverberator preparation allows us to add reverb to our pianos, and exists both as an independent preparation and the last processor in the audio chain accessible in the application footer.

### How to make a Reverberator Preparation

There is both the global Reverberator, which affects all preparations in the Construction Site, and Reverberators as individual preparations, which can be attached to specific preparations. To access the global Reverberator, click the Reverberator button in the lower right-hand corner, between the keyboard and gain meter and below the Compressor button.

To add a Reverberator preparation to the Construction Site, select the “add/copy/paste/align” button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the “Preparation” heading, and select “Reverberator.” You can also simply type the keyboard shortcut SHIFT \+ ‘r,’ and the Reverberator will appear in the Construction site. Double-click on the Reverberator preparation, and you’ll see the pop-up window displayed below.

![][image109]

### Reverberator Parameters

The reverberator in bitKlavier is based on the excellent Dragonfly reverb; please refer to the [Dragonfly manual](https://michaelwillis.github.io/dragonfly-reverb/dragonfly-hall-manual.html) for a complete description of all the parameters.

| VSTs |
| :---- |

### What is it?

New to this version of bitKlavier, users can now incorporate third party VSTs into their bitKlavier pianos. 

See [earlier](#vsts-1) for more information about how to set these up. 

### VST Modifications

Parameters that VSTs expose for automation can be accessed by bitKlavier modification system; simply attach a Modification to the VST and double-click on the Mod triangle to see the available parameters:

![][image110]

| ChucKlavier |
| :---- |

### What is it?

ChucKlavier embeds the [ChucK](https://chuck.stanford.edu/) audio programming language directly into a bitKlavier preparation. Rather than selecting from a fixed set of pre-designed behaviors, you write a ChucK script that runs inside the live audio graph — processing MIDI, generating or shaping audio, computing tuning, and much more. The script executes in a real-time VM; you can recompile and hot-swap it while playback continues without interrupting sound.

ChucKlavier gives bitKlavier an open-ended, programmable layer. If the built-in preparations don't do quite what you need, ChucKlavier lets you build it.

### How to make a ChucKlavier Preparation

Select the "add/copy/paste/align" button at the top of the bitKlavier screen under the "Preparation" heading and select "ChucKlavier." You can also press the `=` key anywhere in the Construction Site to create one instantly. Double-click a ChucKlavier preparation to open its editing window.

![][imageChucKlavier_overview]

### Navigating the ChucKlavier Preparation

#### Code Editor

The large text area on the left is a full-featured ChucK code editor with syntax highlighting. Write your ChucK script here. The editor saves your script continuously into the gallery file as you type, so your code is never lost on close.

#### Status Label

Just above the button row is a status label that shows the result of the last compile. It displays green text on success and orange text with an error message on failure. When a compile error occurs, the offending line in the editor is highlighted in red and scrolled into view.

#### Send to VM

Click **Send to VM** to compile the current script and hot-swap it into the running ChucK VM. The swap is seamless — audio playback continues uninterrupted. If the script does not compile, the VM keeps running the previous script and the error is shown in the status label.

#### Console Button

Click **Console** to open the ChucK output console. The console captures everything printed by `<<<>>>` expressions in your script and displays it as scrolling text. The console floats over the interface, can be dragged by its header strip, and can be closed with its **X** button or the Escape key. A **Clear** button inside the console clears its content.

If you click **Send to VM** while your script contains `<<<>>>` expressions, the console opens automatically. Each time you resend the script, a separator line (`--- <prep>: reload ---`) appears in the console so you can tell where one run ends and the next begins.

When multiple ChucKlavier preps are active, each line of console output is prefixed with a short identifier so you can tell which prep produced it.

![][imageChucKlavier_console]

#### Knob Panel

When your script declares `global float` variables with `//@knob` annotations, they appear as knobs in the panel on the right side of the preparation window. These knobs set the initial value of the corresponding ChucK global and can be connected to Modification preparations for real-time modulation (see **@knob Annotations** below).

![][imageChucKlavier_knobs]

#### Level Meters

Four level meters appear at the edges of the preparation window:

| Meter | Label | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Left outer | External | Audio from an external source (microphone/line in standalone; sidechain in plugin) |
| Left inner | Internal | Audio bussed in from other preparations connected to ChucKlavier |
| Right inner | Send | Volume of ChucKlavier's output routed to connected downstream preparations |
| Right outer | Main | Overall output volume of ChucKlavier |

Click and drag a meter's fader to adjust its level. All four levels are modulatable via bitKlavier's Modification system.

#### Mute and Solo

The **M** (Mute) and **S** (Solo) buttons below the right-side meters work identically to mute/solo on other preparations. Option-click Mute to mute only this preparation (leaving others unaffected). Option-click Solo to solo only this preparation. When a preparation is silenced because another preparation is soloed, its M button blinks.

### Built-in ChucK Globals

bitKlavier automatically populates several global variables in every ChucKlavier script. You do not need to declare these — they are always available:

| Variable | Type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `bkMidiIn` | `global int[4]` | Most recent incoming MIDI message: `[status, data1, data2, channel]` |
| `bkMidiOut` | `global int[4]` | MIDI message to send out: set values then broadcast `bkMidiOutEvent` |
| `bkMidiInEvent` | `global Event` | Signals whenever a new MIDI message arrives |
| `bkMidiOutEvent` | `global Event` | Broadcast to transmit the `bkMidiOut` values downstream |
| `bkTuningTable` | `global float[128]` | bitKlavier's current tuning, as cents offset per MIDI note (0 = equal temperament) |
| `bkTempoBPM` | `global float` | Current host or Synchronic tempo in BPM |

A typical MIDI-responding script waits on `bkMidiInEvent` and inspects `bkMidiIn`:

```chuck
while (true) {
    bkMidiInEvent => now;          // wait for a note
    if (bkMidiIn[0] == 144) {      // note-on (status 144 = 0x90)
        <<< "note:", bkMidiIn[1], "velocity:", bkMidiIn[2] >>>;
    }
}
```

### @knob Annotations

You can expose any `global float` in your script as a knob in the preparation's knob panel by adding a `//@knob` comment on the same line:

```chuck
global float myFilterFreq;  //@knob label="Filter Freq" min=200 max=8000 default=1000
global float myDecay;       //@knob label="Decay" min=0.01 max=2.0 default=0.5
```

The available annotation fields are:

| Field | Default | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `label` | variable name | Display name shown on the knob |
| `min` | 0 | Minimum value |
| `max` | 1 | Maximum value |
| `default` | 0.5 | Initial knob value |

After adding or changing `//@knob` annotations, click **Send to VM** to rebuild the knob panel. Existing knob connections survive script edits as long as the variable name stays the same.

@knob parameters are fully modulatable. Attach a Modification preparation to the ChucKlavier preparation, double-click the Modification triangle, and you will see all @knob parameters listed alongside the standard level controls. Modulation is applied at audio rate, so even fast LFOs track smoothly.

### The Default Script

A newly created ChucKlavier preparation loads this script:

```chuck
// bitKlavier ChucKlavier default: audio + MIDI passthrough
global int bkMidiIn[4];
global int bkMidiOut[4];
global Event bkMidiInEvent;
global Event bkMidiOutEvent;
global float bkTuningTable[128];
global float bkTempoBPM;

adc => dac;

fun void midiPassthrough() {
    while( true ) {
        bkMidiInEvent => now;
        bkMidiIn[0] => bkMidiOut[0];
        bkMidiIn[1] => bkMidiOut[1];
        bkMidiIn[2] => bkMidiOut[2];
        bkMidiIn[3] => bkMidiOut[3];
        bkMidiOutEvent.broadcast();
    }
}
spork ~ midiPassthrough();

while( true ) { 1::samp => now; }
```

This script passes audio straight through (`adc => dac`) and forwards every incoming MIDI message unchanged. It is a safe starting point that keeps sound flowing while you begin writing your own script.

bitKlavier is an open-source project developed by [Dan Trueman](http://manyarrowsmusic.com/), Mike Mulshine, Davis Polito, and Matt Wang, with Theo Trevisan, Jeff Gordon, Myra Norton, and Katie Chou, at Princeton University. 

This bitKlavier manual is a revision by Myra Norton of an earlier version written by [Noah Fishman](http://www.noahfishmanmusic.com/) and edited by Dan Trueman, Noah Fishman, Mike Mulshine, and Matt Wang. 

[bitKlavier](https://bitklavier.com/) is the software engine that drives the prepared digital piano, running on MacOSX and has been used by dozens of performers—from young students to renowned professionals—in a range of compositions by Trueman and others. 

Development of bitKlavier has been sponsored by the [American Council of Learned Societies](http://www.acls.org/), the [New Jersey State Council on the Arts](http://www.artscouncil.nj.gov/), and Princeton University’s [Center for Digital Humanities](https://cdh.princeton.edu/), [Council on Science and Technology](https://cst.princeton.edu/), [Council of the Humanities](https://humanities.princeton.edu/), and [Department of Music](https://music.princeton.edu/).

bitKlavier is an [open-source project](https://github.com/Princeton-CDH/bitKlavier), created in C++ using [JUCE](https://juce.com/). Developers interested in joining the project can of course download the source from the [GitHub](https://github.com/Princeton-CDH/bitKlavier) site. | Temperament | U | m2 | M2 | m3 | M3 | P4 | a4/d5 | P5 | m6 | M6 | m7 | M7 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Just  | 1/1 | 16/15 | 9/8 | 6/5 | 5/4 | 4/3 | 7/5 | 3/2 | 8/5 | 5/3 | 7/4 | 15/8 |

For the historical temperaments, visit [Carey Beebe’s wonderful website](http://www.hpschd.nu/index.html?nav/nav-4.html&t/welcome.html&http://www.hpschd.nu/tech/tmp/spiral.html), which describes all of the systems in bitKlavier, including how they are actually executed. See Kyle Gann’s [page](https://www.kylegann.com/wtp.html) for information about the La Monte Young “Well Tuned Piano” tuning, and [this article](https://www.keyboardmag.com/artists/lou-harrison-explorations-in-just-intonation-and-temperaments-on-the-keyboard) by Giacomo Fiore and Larry Polansky for more about the “Harrison Strict” tuning.  
 

### Sample Library Formats

bitKlavier can work with: 

* Soundfonts (sf2 and sfz, placed in the \~/Documents/bitKlavier/soundfonts folder)   
* raw samples (wav files placed in the \~/Documents/bitKlavier/samples folder) following a simple structure:

#### Folders:

##### “main”

These are the primary samples for the instrument. Sample files should be named ***\[Note\]\[Octave\]v\[Velocity\].wav***, e.g. “F\#6v5.wav” and will be assigned to the note and octave specified by the name. bitKlavier will transpose from that root note normally. There can be even just one sample in this folder, which will be mapped to the full keyboard, or many as in the Yamaha\_Default soundset.

##### “hammer”

These samples are played on noteOff, and are typically the sound of the hammer falling back into place. Hammer release sounds should be named ***rel\[key number\].wav***, e.g. “rel76.wav” and will be mapped to the keys accordingly.

##### “resonance” 

These samples are played on noteOff, and are typically the quiet resonance that is created when keys are released on an acoustic piano. Resonance release samples should be named ***harm\[Note\]\[Octave\]v\[Velocity\].wav***, e.g. “harmD\#sv3.wav” and will be mapped to the full keyboard accordingly.

##### “pedal”

Named pedalD1 (pedal depressed) and pedalU1 (pedal released), and are mapped to the sustain pedal.
